headline: AI used for missile guidance software by Yemen cell, Anthropic reports
summary: Operators reportedly used Anthropic's Claude Code to simulate trajectories and develop software for guided rockets, compressing specialist engineering work into an AI-assisted workflow.
details: A cell in northern Yemen has reportedly used Anthropic's Claude Code to develop software for guided rockets, a long-range ballistic missile, and a hypersonic glide vehicle concept. This marks one of the clearest examples of generative AI being applied directly to conventional weapons development.

Operators ran multiple Claude instances simultaneously, dividing tasks between coding, research, and technical review. This workflow allowed a small group to replicate functions normally distributed across specialist engineering teams, accelerating the development cycle.

Projects included guidance software for tactical rockets, a ballistic missile exceeding 2,000 km range, and a hypersonic glide vehicle variant. The operators also used Claude for reinforcement learning to tune flight-control algorithms and developed six-degree-of-freedom trajectory simulations.

The group reportedly test-fired a guided rocket, which appears to have failed. However, they used Claude to analyze launch telemetry within hours, demonstrating how the AI was integrated into an iterative weapons-engineering cycle.

Anthropic found no evidence that the group succeeded in fielding an operational weapon. However, by the time their accounts were disrupted, the operators had assembled an offline engineering toolkit that no longer depended on access to Claude.

Anthropic's safeguards blocked numerous requests, but operators adapted by obscuring end-use intentions and dividing work across separate conversations. The company subsequently banned the linked accounts.

headline_marked: [[Your car is selling your data]] to insurers and brokers, report reveals
headline: Your car is selling your data to insurers and brokers, report reveals
summary: Automakers collect vast amounts of driving data, often without clear consent, and sell it to third parties, impacting insurance rates and privacy.
details: General Motors was recently fined by the FTC for selling customer driving data to brokers like LexisNexis and Verisk, who then provided risk profiles to insurance companies. Many drivers were unaware their data was being collected through services like OnStar's Smart Driver feature, leading to potential insurance rate hikes.

A 2023 Mozilla Foundation study found that every major automaker has "horrible privacy and security" policies. Customers are often overwhelmed by multiple, overlapping privacy agreements for various car-related services, making it difficult to understand the extent of data collection.

Consumer Reports investigations corroborate these findings, indicating that nearly every automaker selling cars in the U.S. collects and shares "driver behavior data" with other companies. Unlike smartphones, cars have less intuitive privacy controls, with data collection spread across multiple systems.

While legislation like the proposed DRIVER Act aims to give owners more control, it may still permit automakers to sell data, which privacy advocates argue is insufficient. True privacy would require preventing excessive collection rather than just offering difficult-to-use access and deletion rights.
